saa-ini-157.text: A web application behind a Application Load Balancer is suffering a brute force attack on the login form: the same set of IP addresses is sending thousands of login attempts per minute. The team wants to automatically block, for a period, IPs that exceed a certain number of requests in a short time interval, without blocking legitimate users.?
options: AWS WAF with a rate-based rule (rate-based rule), which automatically blocks IP addresses that exceed a requirement limit defined in a time window
Increase the size of the instances EC2 behind the ALB to support more requests
Configure a Security Group which blocks all entry traffic at the door 443
Configure the Amazon GuardDuty to automatically block suspicious traffic
saa-ini-157.explanation: The rules based on the rate of AWS WAF monitor the amount of IP requests from origin in a time window and automatically block (for a configurable period) IPs that exceed the defined limit, mitigating brute force attacks without affecting legitimate users.
saa-ini-157.hint: Think about the resource of AWS WAF allowing you to automatically lock IP addresses that exceed a number of requests in a time window.
optionRationales: The rules based on the rate of AWS WAF monitor the amount of IP requests from origin in a time window and automatically block (for a configurable period) IPs that exceed the defined limit, mitigating brute force attacks without affecting legitimate users.
Lock the whole door 443 would prevent access of TODOS users, including legitimate ones — is not a selective solution against abusive IPs.
Increasing computing capacity does not stop the brute force attack — it would just make it more expensive to absorb it without solving the problem.
The GuardDuty detects and generates threats alerts, but does not block traffic directly in the network layer/load balancer — this blocking action is the role of the WAF.

saa-ini-158.text: A company operates a critical financial application and wants advanced protection against volumetric DDoS attacks on layers 3/4 and 7, including access to a specialized DDoS response team (DRT) and cost protection against escalating peaks caused by an attack. AWS Shield Standard, enabled by default and free, already offers some protection, but does not cover these additional features. AWS meets this requirement?
options: AWS Shield Standard, which already provides access to DRT and cost protection
AWS Shield Advanced, which offers advanced protection against DDoS, access to DDoS Response Team (DRT) and cost protection against escalating peaks during attacks
AWS WAF, configured in isolation without the Shield Advanced
Amazon GuardDuty with all detectors enabled
saa-ini-158.explanation: Correct. AWS Shield Advanced, a paid service, adds advanced protection against large-scale DDoS attacks, access to specialized team DRT and cost protection against escalating peaks caused by attacks.
saa-ini-158.hint: Think about the level of protection against DDoS AWS, payment, which adds access to a specialized response and cost protection team against escalating peaks during attacks.
optionRationales: Correct. AWS Shield Advanced, a paid service, adds advanced protection against large-scale DDoS attacks, access to specialized team DRT and cost protection against escalating peaks caused by attacks.
The AWS WAF protects against holdings in the application layer, such as SQL injection e XSS, but does not provide access to the DDoS Response Team or cost protection against escalating peaks.
The GuardDuty is a threat detection service — it does not provide DDoS mitigation capability or access to DRT.
The Shield Standard is the basic, free and automatically enabled protection for all customers — it does NOT include access to DRT no cost protection, benefits exclusively from Advanced level.

saa-ini-159.text: A company uses AWS KMS to encrypt sensitive data with a customer-managed key (customer managed key) - CMK). By security policy, the underlying cryptographic material of the key must be rotated annually, but the team does not want to manually re-encrypt all existing data at each rotation, nor to update key references in their applications. KMS meets this requirement?
options: Use only keys managed by AWS (AWS managed keys), which cannot have the rotation configured by the customer
Create a new one CMK every year and manually re-encrypt all data with the new key
Enable automatic key rotation at CMK, which generates new cryptographic material annually maintaining the same ID/ARN of the key, without requiring re-encryption of existing data
Disable encryption and apply encryption at the application level
saa-ini-159.explanation: Correct. Automatic key rotation of the KMS generates new backend cryptographic material periodically (annually), but maintains the same ID/ARN of CMK — o KMS continues to know how to decipher old data with the previous material, without the need to re-encrypt existing data or change references in the application.
saa-ini-159.hint: Think about the resource of KMS which automatically generates new cryptographic material for a customer-managed key periodically, without changing the ID/ARN of the key nor require re-cryption of data.
optionRationales: Correct. Automatic key rotation of the KMS generates new backend cryptographic material periodically (annually), but maintains the same ID/ARN of CMK — o KMS continues to know how to decipher old data with the previous material, without the need to re-encrypt existing data or change references in the application.
This is exactly the manual work of re-crypting and updating references that the team wants to avoid — automatic rotation resolves this in a transparent way.

The AWS managed keys already rotate automatically every year, but the scenario explicitly requires the use of a customer-managed key (CMK) — and the question is about the rotational resource applicable to that CMK.
Remove encryption managed by KMS eliminates your benefits completely and does not meet the requirement of periodic key rotation.

saa-ini-160.text: An application stores database credentials Amazon RDS The security team requires that these credentials be removed from the code, stored securely and rotated automatically in a regular interval, without the need to manually change the password in the database and in the application to each rotation. AWS fully meets this requirement?
options: Store credentials as environment variables encrypted in a function Lambda
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, in the Standard layer, without any additional configuration
Create a Bucket S3 private to store a configuration file with credentials
AWS Secrets Manager, which stores credentials securely and encryptedly, and can rotate them automatically within a defined interval, updating both the stored secret and the password in the database
saa-ini-160.explanation: Correct. AWS Secrets Manager encrypted credentials storage and offers automatic rotation integrated with databases RDS, updating the bank password and the secret stored simultaneously, without manual intervention.
saa-ini-160.hint: Think of the service of AWS dedicated to secure storage of credentials that can rotate them automatically, updating both the secret and password in the database.
optionRationales: Correct. AWS Secrets Manager encrypted credentials storage and offers automatic rotation integrated with databases RDS, updating the bank password and the secret stored simultaneously, without manual intervention.

The Parameter Store in the Standard layer can store encrypted secrets via KMS, but does not offer integrated automatic rotation that updates the password in the database — this feature is Secrets Manager.
This would also require updating manually both the environment variable and the database password at each rotation — does not meet the full automatic rotation requirement.
Store credentials in a file at S3 does not offer automatic rotation and is a less secure standard than a dedicated secret management service.

saa-ini-161.text: A company wants to continuously monitor its accounts AWS in search of malicious or unauthorized activities — as calls for API anomalous, communication with IP addresses known to host malware, or instances EC2 committed mining cryptocurrency — automatically analyzing sources like CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs, without needing to deploy agents or own infrastructure. AWS meets this requirement?
options: AWS CloudTrail, configured to generate alerts automatically
AWS Config, which assesses the conformity of resource configuration with defined rules

Amazon GuardDuty, a threat detection service that continuously analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs using threat intelligence and machine learning, without requiring agents or additional infrastructure
Amazon Inspector, evaluating software vulnerabilities in instances EC2 and images of containers
saa-ini-161.explanation: Correct. Amazon GuardDuty continuously analyzes data sources as CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs, applying threat intelligence and machine learning to identify malicious activities, such as cryptocurrency mining or communication with malicious IPs, without the need for agents.
saa-ini-161.hint: Think of the threat detection service of the AWS that continuously analyzes logs as CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and DNS, using threat intelligence and machine learning, without requiring agents.
optionRationales: Correct. Amazon GuardDuty continuously analyzes data sources as CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs, applying threat intelligence and machine learning to identify malicious activities, such as cryptocurrency mining or communication with malicious IPs, without the need for agents.

The AWS Config checks whether the resource configuration is in accordance with defined rules — it does not analyze logs for malicious activity patterns such as cryptocurrency mining or calls from API anomalous.
The Inspector focus on vulnerability assessment in workloads — not on continuous analysis of account activity logs for threat detection.

The CloudTrail records the activity of API, but does not analyze these logs in search of threats using threat intelligence and machine learning — this is the role of GuardDuty, which uses the CloudTrail as one of your data sources.

saa-ini-162.text: A company stores large volumes of files in the Amazon S3 and suspect that some of these files may contain sensitive data, such as credit card numbers or identifiable personal information (PII), stored without proper control. The team wants a service that uses machine learning and pattern matching to automatically discover and classify these sensitive data within the newsletters S3. What is the service of AWS meets this requirement?
options: Amazon Macie, using machine learning and pattern matching to discover, classify and protect sensitive data (such as PII and financial data) stored in Amazon S3
Amazon Athena, carrying out consultations SQL manuals on the files of the S3
Amazon Rekognition, which analyzes images and videos
AWS Glue Data Catalog, which only catalogues metadata of data schemes
saa-ini-162.explanation: Correct. Amazon Macie uses machine learning and pattern matching techniques to scan buckets S3, identifying and automatically classifying sensitive data as identifiable personal information (PII) and credit card numbers.
saa-ini-162.hint: Think of the service of AWS using machine learning to automatically discover and classify sensitive data (such as PII) stored in Amazon S3.
optionRationales: Correct. Amazon Macie uses machine learning and pattern matching techniques to scan buckets S3, identifying and automatically classifying sensitive data as identifiable personal information (PII) and credit card numbers.
The Athena allows you to consult data via SQL, but does not automatically discover and classify sensitive data patterns using machine learning on all the bucks.
The Glue Data Catalog manages metadata about data structure/scheme — it does not classify the sensitivity of data content.
Rekognition is focused on image and video analysis — not discovery of sensitive text data, such as PII, in objects of the S3.

saa-ini-163.text: A platform team wants developers to create their own roles and policies IAM for your projects, but you need to ensure that, regardless of the permissions a developer grants to a roll, this roll is NUNCA may exceed a centrally defined maximum set of permissions (for example, you may never access resources from other teams or change account security settings). IAM allows to define this maximum effective permissions for entities created by other users?
options: Resource tags combined with tag-based policies
Groups of IAM, which only group users for allocation of common policies
Permission Boundaries, a managed policy that defines the MAXIMUM set of permissions that an entity IAM may have, regardless of the identity-based policies attached to it
Service Control Policies (SCPs) applied only to the root account (management account))
saa-ini-163.explanation: Right. Permission Boundaries define the maximum ceiling of effective permissions of an entity IAM (user or role): even if identity-based policies grant wider permissions, effective access never exceeds what the limit allows.
saa-ini-163.hint: Think about the resource of IAM which defines the maximum limit of permissions that an entity may have, complementing (but not replacing) identity-based policies.
optionRationales: Right. Permission Boundaries define the maximum ceiling of effective permissions of an entity IAM (user or role): even if identity-based policies grant wider permissions, effective access never exceeds what the limit allows.

SCPs act at the level of AWS Organizations, restricting what whole accounts can do — the scenario describes limiting individual roles/users created within the UMA other users, which is the purpose of permission bonds.
Groups of IAM are an organizational resource to assign shared policies to users — they do not impose a maximum ceiling of permissions for roles created independently by others.
Tag-based policies may restrict access to resources with specific tags, but do not set a general ceiling of maximum permissions, regardless of what identity policies grant.

saa-ini-164.text: A company needs to continuously ensure that all volumes EBS The team also wants to maintain a history of changes in the configuration of resources for audit purposes. AWS meets these requirements for continuous conformity assessment and configuration history?
options: AWS Config, which continuously evaluates the configuration of resources against defined rules (such as 'volumes' EBS must be encrypted'), maintains a history of configuration changes and can trigger automatic remediations via SSM Automation
Amazon CloudWatch Events (EventBridge) configured in isolation
AWS Trusted Advisor, at the Basic support level
Amazon Inspector, configured to scan volumes EBS
saa-ini-164.explanation: Correct. AWS Config continuously evaluates remedies against compliance rules (such as requiring volume encryption) EBS), maintains a detailed history of configuration changes for audit, and can trigger automatic remediation actions using the SSM Automation.
saa-ini-164.hint: Think of the service of AWS which continuously evaluates whether resources are in accordance with defined rules (such as volume encryption), maintains configuration history and can trigger automatic remedial actions.
optionRationales: Correct. AWS Config continuously evaluates remedies against compliance rules (such as requiring volume encryption) EBS), maintains a detailed history of configuration changes for audit, and can trigger automatic remediation actions using the SSM Automation.

The EventBridge route events between services and can trigger actions, but does not continuously evaluate the configuration of resources against compliance rules nor maintains a configuration history.
The basic level of Trusted Advisor offers only a limited set of checks and does not provide continuous evaluation of custom rules, auto repair or configuration history.

The Inspector evaluate workloads (instances) EC2, container images, Lambda) as for software vulnerabilities and network exposure — general non-conformity of resource configuration, such as encryption, with history of changes.

saa-ini-165.text: The security team suspects that an instance EC2 within a VPC is communicating with a suspicious external IP address, but needs to confirm this by analyzing network traffic metadata (origin, destination, ports, protocol, and whether the traffic has been accepted or rejected) that enters and exits the network interfaces of the VPC — without needing to capture the content (payload) of the packages. AWS captures this type of information on network traffic in a VPC?
options: Amazon CloudWatch Logs, configured in isolation without any additional source
AWS X-Ray, tracking requests through microservices
AWS CloudTrail, which records calls from API made on account

VPC Flow Logs, which capture metadata about IP traffic entering and leaving the network interfaces of a VPC (origin, destination, ports, protocol, accepted/rejected action), without capturing the contents of the packages
saa-ini-165.explanation: Right. VPC Flow Logs record metadata on IP traffic in network interfaces from VPC — including IPs and ports of origin/destiny, protocol, number of packages/bytes and whether traffic was ACCEPT or REJECT — without capturing the payload of packages.
saa-ini-165.hint: Think of the resource of AWS that records metadata on IP traffic (origin, destination, port, protocol, accepted/rejected) that enters and exits the network interfaces of a VPC.
optionRationales: Right. VPC Flow Logs record metadata on IP traffic in network interfaces from VPC — including IPs and ports of origin/destiny, protocol, number of packages/bytes and whether traffic was ACCEPT or REJECT — without capturing the payload of packages.
The CloudTrail records management activity/API (who called which API), non-traffic metadata of network packages between instances.
The CloudWatch Logs is a log storage destination/service; network traffic metadata itself need to be generated by VPC Flow Logs, which can then be sent to CloudWatch Logs.
X-Ray tracks application level requests between distributed services — it does not capture raw IP traffic metadata at the level of network interfaces of the VPC.

saa-ini-166.text: A company needs to enable HTTPS in one Application Load Balancer and in a distribution of CloudFront, using certificates SSL/TLS The team wants to avoid the manual process of purchasing, uploading and renewing certificates before they expire, preferring a service that provides and renews publicly reliable certificates automatically, integrating natively with these services. AWS meets this requirement?
options: AWS KMS, creating a symmetrical key to represent the certificate

AWS Certificate Manager (ACM), which automatically supplies, manages and renews certificates SSL/TLS public, integrating directly with ALB, CloudFront and other services, without additional cost for public certificates
AWS Secrets Manager, storing the certificate as a rotating secret
Make manual upload of certificates from an external certifying authority to the IAM, renewing them manually each year
saa-ini-166.explanation: Correct. AWS Certificate Manager provide certificates SSL/TLS public for free, renews them automatically before maturity, and integrates natively with services such as ALB and CloudFront, eliminating manual certificate management.
saa-ini-166.hint: Think of the service of AWS providing and renewing certificates automatically SSL/TLS public, with native integration to services such as the ALB and the CloudFront.
optionRationales: Correct. AWS Certificate Manager provide certificates SSL/TLS public for free, renews them automatically before maturity, and integrates natively with services such as ALB and CloudFront, eliminating manual certificate management.
The KMS manage encryption keys to encrypt data — it does not issue or manage certificates SSL/TLS for endpoints HTTPS.
This is exactly the manual process that the team wants to avoid — the ACM automates the issue and renewal of certificates.

The Secrets Manager rotates secrets as database credentials via functions Lambda — it has not been designed to issue/renew certificates TLS publicly reliable nor for native termination integration HTTPS with ALB/CloudFront.

saa-ini-167.text: A company wants to ensure, at the account level and in the pocket, that no object or pocket of the Amazon S3 can be accidentally made public by a developer — even if someone incorrectly configures a ACL or bucket policy allowing public access. The team wants a centralized control that blocks this type of configuration, regardless of other policies. S3 meets this requirement?
options: Encrypt all objects with SSE-KMS
A Bucket policy that explicitly denies the main "*"
S3 Block Public Access, configured at the account and/or bucket level, which superimposes ACLs and Bucket policies to prevent resources S3 become public, even if future settings try to allow this
Enable bucket versioning
saa-ini-167.explanation: Correct. S3 Block Public Access can be enabled at the account or pocket level and superimposes (replaces) ACLs and Bucket policies that attempt to grant public access, functioning as a centralized lock against accidental, current or future public settings.
saa-ini-167.hint: Think about the resource of S3, configurable at account level or pocket, which superimposes (substitute) configurations of ACL and Bucket policies to prevent resources from becoming public.
optionRationales: Correct. S3 Block Public Access can be enabled at the account or pocket level and superimposes (replaces) ACLs and Bucket policies that attempt to grant public access, functioning as a centralized lock against accidental, current or future public settings.

A bucket policy denying "*" in a specific bucket may be misconfigured or simply not exist in another bucket — it does not offer overlay at account level that prevents future public settings in all bucks.
Versioning preserves the history of versions of objects — has no relation to the control of public accessibility of objects.
Encryption protects the confidentiality of data at rest, but does not prevent a bucket/object from being made publicly accessible via ACLs or Bucket Policies.

saa-ini-168.text: A company uses several security services from AWS — GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, AWS Config — each generating its own discoveries (findings) in separate consoles. The security team wants a single centralized panel that automatically adds, organizes and prioritizes the discoveries of all these services, in addition to evaluating the account's overall security posture in relation to standards such as the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark. AWS meets this requirement?
options: AWS Trusted Advisor, which shows general cost and performance recommendations
Amazon CloudWatch Dashboards, manually created for each security service
AWS Organizations, setting up an audit account

AWS Security Hub, which adds, organizes and automatically prioritizes multiple service security discoveries (GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Config, etc.) in a centralized panel, in addition to evaluating the account against safety standards such as the CIS Benchmark
saa-ini-168.explanation: Correct. AWS Security Hub automatically centralizes and correlates security discoveries of various services of AWS (GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Config, among others) in a single panel, in addition to continuously evaluating the account in relation to safety standards such as the CIS AWS Benchmark Foundations.
saa-ini-168.hint: Think of the service of AWS which functions as a central panel that aggregates and prioritizes discoveries (findings) of other security services, such as GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie, and evaluates the count against patterns such as the CIS Benchmark.
optionRationales: Correct. AWS Security Hub automatically centralizes and correlates security discoveries of various services of AWS (GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Config, among others) in a single panel, in addition to continuously evaluating the account in relation to safety standards such as the CIS AWS Benchmark Foundations.
Building dashboards manually for each service requires significant manual effort and does not offer automatic aggregation, prioritization and evaluation against standards that Security Hub provides.
The Trusted Advisor provides general checks of good practice in various categories, but does not specifically aggregate the findings of GuardDuty/Inspector/Macie/Configure a unified security vision.
The AWS Organizations manages the multi-account structure and policies (such as SCPs) — it does not aggregate and prioritize, by itself, security discoveries of other services.
